title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 262
paragraphs: The pig is accounted an abominable animal by the Egyptians; first, if any of them in passing touches a pig, he goes into the river and dips himself immediately in the water along with his garments. Second, swineherds, though they be native Egyptians, unlike all others do not enter any of the temples in Egypt, nor is anyone willing to give his daughter in marriage to one of them or to take a wife from among them; the swineherds marry their own daughters to each other and take wives from among one another. Now the Egyptians do not think it right to sacrifice swine to the other gods; but to the Moon and to Dionysus alone — at the same time and on the same full moon — they sacrifice swine and then eat their flesh. As to why, when they abominate swine at all their other festivals, they sacrifice them at this one, there is a story told by the Egyptians; and though I know this story, it is not a seemly one for me to tell. The sacrifice of the swine to the Moon is performed as follows: when the priest has slain the victim, he puts together the end of the tail, the spleen, and the caul, and covers them with the whole of the fat around the paunch, and then he offers them with fire; and the rest of the flesh they eat on that day of full moon on which they held the sacrifice, but on any day after this they will not taste of it. The poor among them, by reason of their scanty means, shape pigs out of dough, bake them, and offer these as sacrifices.
